wordsPreamble:
- Milan speaks standard Italian with a northern accent. The old Milanese dialect survives mostly among older people and in a handful of phrases everyone knows.
- An *s* between vowels is buzzed like a z here: *casa* sounds like “kaza.” Every letter is still pronounced, and double consonants are held longer.
- English is common in the centre, in business and fashion, and in hotels. Milan is Italy’s working city and moves quickly, so keep exchanges short and polite.
- Greet people entering a shop or bar, and again on the way out. Coffee is drunk standing at the counter, and fast.

words.context: Still buongiorno until mid-afternoon. Buon pomeriggio exists but is rarely said to strangers.

words.groupNote: Buonasera starts in the afternoon, from about four. Milanese often clip both to ’giorno and ’sera.

words.context: Hello and goodbye, for friends and peers. Among friends you will also hear Uè (weh), a loud all-purpose Milanese hey.
Buona giornata (have a good day) on the way out is just as common, and Milanese shopkeepers will say it first.
Three syllables, not two. Grazie mille is a thousand thanks.
Often answered in English before you finish. Milan does business in it.
For a real apology. For a bump on the metro, scusi is the word.
Say it on a packed tram or metro before you move toward the doors.
Milan eats dinner around eight, earlier than Rome. Book on Fridays and Saturdays.
If you’re warm and kind, this is enough to get by. More polite version: Il menù, per favore.
The clink at aperitivo. Salute (sah-LOO-teh) is the plainer toast, and also what you say after a sneeze.
More polite version: Il conto, per favore. At a busy coffee bar, pay first at the till and hand the receipt to the barista.
A per-person charge for bread and the table, printed on the menu. Legitimate. At aperitivo the drink price usually includes the snacks.
On the metro you can tap a contactless bank card at the gates instead of buying one. Keep it to tap out.
Bars expect you to buy something first. A coffee at the counter is the usual price of entry.

words.groupNote: Also Signori (men) and Signore (women), one vowel apart on adjacent doors.

words.context: Not to be confused with ATM, the city’s transport company, whose logo is on every tram stop. Decline the offer to charge you in dollars.
Cards are accepted almost everywhere, including for a single espresso.
Worth a few coins for market stalls, newsstands and the odd old bar.
Charged by law. Say no grazie if you brought one.
Dialect for signora: the well-dressed, well-off older Milanese lady, fur coat in winter, small dog, firm opinions, coffee at the same bar every day. Said with affection, and some caution.
A braggart, roughly one who drools while boasting. AC Milan fans use it for Inter fans, and Inter fans have adopted it with pride. The two clubs share San Siro stadium.
“Milan to drink”: a 1980s advertising slogan for Ramazzotti, a Milanese herbal liqueur, that became the name for the city’s high-living decade, and for the bribery scandals that ended it.
Aperitivo plus cena, dinner: an early-evening drink with a buffet substantial enough to replace the meal. The bars along the Navigli canals are where it is taken most seriously.
Dialect for “I’ll take care of it.” The Milanese motto of quiet self-reliance and getting on with the job, quoted with pride and, increasingly, with irony.
